Common chimpanzees exhibit a life-history profile that reflects their prolonged developmental period and complex social structure. Field studies at Ngogo in Kibale National Park have documented newborn infants with a wet weight at birth of 1821 grams [Wwb = 1821 grams], a mass that facilitates a relatively rapid early growth phase under intensive maternal care. The immature female reaches puberty at 3376 days since birth [tp = 3376 days since birth], a milestone that marks the onset of gonadal activity and the beginning of cyclical hormonal changes at a temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. Core body temperature in this species, typically maintained around 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], provides the thermal context for these developmental events. Gestation itself lasts 229 days [tg = 229 days], a duration typical for a primate of this body size and consistent with the substantial neonatal mass requiring extended in utero development before the live birth event occurs at a temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C].

In terms of reproductive output, chimpanzees are characterized by an exceptionally slow pace of life. The maximum reproductive rate under the species' normal thermoregulatory regime of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C] translates to a single offspring approximately every 840 days. In naturalistic terms, a female typically produces a single infant per birth event [N_R_i = single infant per birth event], with approximately 0.43 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.43 litters per year], reflecting the extensive period of lactation and infant dependency that follows parturition. This low reproductive tempo is compensated by high offspring survivorship in stable environments. The energetic demands of gestation and lactation are substantial, and the female must allocate considerable resources to the nursing offspring before she can resume cycling and conceive again, a pattern that underscores the trade-off between maternal investment and future fecundity.

Adulthood is characterized by a pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass attained by individuals in the wild, reaches 44984 grams [Wwi = 44984 grams], a value that places Pan troglodytes among the largest living primates and reflects the high energetic demands of their frugivorous diet and social dominance hierarchies. Males often surpass females in this metric due to both physiological and social factors. The ultimate body length of 78 centimeters [Li = 78 centimeters] provides a robust structural frame for an animal that engages in both terrestrial knuckle-walking and arboreal climbing, with recorded values spanning from 63.5 to 92.5 centimeters (63.5-92.5 centimeters) [Li = 63.5-92.5 centimeters] across different populations. This variation likely reflects local ecological conditions, including food availability and habitat quality. The species' relatively large body size compared to other hominids confers advantages in competitive interactions but also requires a substantial daily caloric intake to sustain resting metabolic demands.

The weaning process marks a critical transition from maternal dependency to nutritional independence. Under typical thermal conditions of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], weaning occurs at 1111 days since birth [tx = 1111 days since birth], an extended period of suckling that is among the longest documented for any non-human primate. This prolonged nursing phase coincides with the gradual introduction of solid foods, as the offspring learns to identify and process the diverse fruits, leaves, and insects that comprise the adult diet. The cessation of lactation allows the mother to redirect energetic resources toward her own somatic condition and, ultimately, toward the next pregnancy. The weaning age also correlates with the development of the juvenile's nervous system and the acquisition of essential foraging skills learned through observational learning within the community.

Longevity in this species reflects the slow life-history strategy common among large-brained primates. The maximum lifespan is approximately 59.4 years [am = approximately 59.4 years], a figure derived from long-term records of known individuals in both wild and captive settings when maintained at a typical body temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. This extended period of survival is accompanied by a gradual process of reproductive senescence in females, who may experience several years of post-reproductive life, a trait shared with humans and a few other cetaceans. The physiological mechanisms underlying this longevity include efficient cellular repair processes and a remarkably slow age-related decline in immune function compared to mammals of similar body mass. Older individuals often serve as repositories of ecological knowledge, guiding the group to fruiting trees and water sources during periods of resource scarcity.
